proposedTopics.title: Opcodes Deep Dive
proposedTopics.description: The EVM at the raw opcode level: gas per opcode, stack/memory/storage/transient ops, the CALL and CREATE families, external-code and halting opcodes — deeper than the Phase-1 interpreter sketch.

proposedTopics.title: Yul & Inline Assembly
proposedTopics.description: Yul as Solidity's low-level dialect: syntax, the solc memory model (free memory pointer, scratch space), calldata decoding, reverting with data, and standalone Yul objects.

proposedTopics.title: Huff & Hand-Written Bytecode
proposedTopics.description: Huff — opcodes plus macros and manual stack manipulation — for hand-built dispatchers and gas-critical primitives: macros, stack effects, scoped labels, and when the effort pays off. The current huff2 compiler does not yet implement jump tables.

proposedTopics.title: Opcode gas accounting
proposedTopics.description: Opcode charges combine schedule groups with operation-specific dynamic components: account and storage access can be cold or warm (EIP-2929), memory growth charges the increase in the memory-cost function, and SSTORE depends on original, current, and new values. EIP-150 caps ordinary CALL-family forwarded gas at all but one sixty-fourth of the available gas after call costs. If a frame cannot pay a charge, it halts exceptionally: that frame's state changes are discarded and it returns no remaining gas.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/gas-trace.md take a short, compiler-emitted opcode trace, record the pre-op stack/memory/access state, and hand-compute each charge from the Yellow Paper plus current EIPs; keep the trace and arithmetic beside test/phase08/GasTrace.t.sol. Done when: the sum matches the trace interval you defined and you can isolate every cold-access or memory-expansion component without counting test-harness overhead.

proposedTopics.title: Stack, arithmetic & bitwise opcodes
proposedTopics.description: The stack holds at most 1024 256-bit words. PUSH0 pushes zero; PUSH1–PUSH32 push 1–32 immediate bytes; DUP1–DUP16 copy and SWAP1–SWAP16 reorder accessible stack items. Arithmetic includes ADD/MUL/SUB/DIV/SDIV/MOD/SMOD/EXP/ADDMOD/MULMOD; comparisons include LT/GT/SLT/SGT/EQ/ISZERO; AND/OR/XOR/NOT/BYTE/SHL/SHR/SAR operate on bits. Signed opcodes interpret the same 256 bits as two's-complement values.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: on evm.codes' playground assemble PUSH1 0x03 PUSH1 0x02 ADD and one signed vs unsigned case (e.g. SDIV of a negative), recording each in contracts/phase08/stack-ops.md. Done when: you can predict the stack after each opcode and explain why DIV by zero yields 0 rather than reverting.

proposedTopics.title: Memory opcodes & expansion
proposedTopics.description: Memory is a volatile, zero-initialized byte array. MLOAD reads 32 bytes, MSTORE writes 32 bytes, MSTORE8 writes one byte, and MSIZE reports the active-memory size in bytes. The active range rounds up to 32-byte words; expanding from a to b words charges Cmem(b)−Cmem(a), where Cmem(x)=3x+⌊x²/512⌋. A high offset therefore pays for the entire newly activated range.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/Mem.sol write an assembly function that MSTOREs a value at 0x80 and MLOADs it back, plus one that MSTORE8s a single byte; test in test/phase08/Mem.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and you can explain, from gas, why writing at offset 0x2000 costs far more than at 0x80.

proposedTopics.title: Storage & transient opcodes
proposedTopics.description: SLOAD costs 2100 gas for a cold slot and 100 once warm. SSTORE metering depends on the slot's original, current, and new values under EIP-2200, with a 2100 first-touch surcharge under EIP-2929 and transaction refunds capped to one fifth of gas used under EIP-3529. TLOAD and TSTORE each cost 100 gas, share contract-owned transient state across its frames, journal writes across reverts, and discard all transient state at transaction end; TSTORE is forbidden in a static context.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/Transient08.sol implement a reentrancy lock with tstore/tload and tests in test/phase08/Transient08.t.sol that reenter and that call the guarded entry twice sequentially in one transaction. Done when: forge test proves reentrancy reverts, the same-transaction second call succeeds after the first returns, and a fresh transaction succeeds.

proposedTopics.title: The CALL family opcodes
proposedTopics.description: CALL executes target code with the target's state context, msg.sender set to the current account, and an explicit value. DELEGATECALL executes target code in the caller's state context while preserving the current frame's sender and value. STATICCALL enters a static context in which state-changing operations fail. CALLCODE is the legacy call variant that keeps the caller's state context but replaces sender/value semantics differently. EIP-150 caps requested forwarded gas after call costs; value-bearing CALL also receives the specified stipend.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/CallFamily.sol implement one function per opcode (call/delegatecall/staticcall) and prove in test/phase08/CallFamily.t.sol how each sees storage and msg.sender. Done when: forge test passes and you can state why a delegatecall to attacker code is a full takeover of your storage.

proposedTopics.title: CREATE & CREATE2 opcodes
proposedTopics.description: Both instructions execute init code whose successful output becomes the account's runtime code. CREATE derives the address from keccak256(RLP(sender, sender_nonce))[12:] and is precomputable when that nonce is known. CREATE2 derives it from keccak256(0xff ‖ sender ‖ salt ‖ keccak256(init_code))[12:], binding the address to the sender, salt, and complete init-code bytes, including encoded constructor arguments.

proposedTopics.title: Context, external-code & halting opcodes
proposedTopics.description: EXTCODESIZE/EXTCODECOPY inspect another account's code. EXTCODEHASH returns zero for a nonexistent or EIP-161-empty account, and keccak256(empty bytes) for an existing account without code. RETURNDATASIZE/RETURNDATACOPY expose the previous subcall's output buffer. LOG0–LOG4 charge 375 base, 375 per topic, and 8 per data byte, plus memory expansion. RETURN and REVERT both return a memory range; REVERT rolls back the frame without consuming all remaining gas, while an invalid instruction halts exceptionally and leaves no gas in that frame.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/CodeProbe.sol write assembly using extcodesize and extcodehash on a target address, plus a function that emits a LOG with two topics; test in test/phase08/CodeProbe.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and you can explain why extcodesize == 0 inside a contract's own constructor makes 'is-EOA' checks bypassable.

proposedTopics.title: Building an EVM interpreter from scratch
proposedTopics.description: Implementing a bounded interpreter makes the execution model concrete: fetch/decode/execute over bytecode with a program counter, 256-bit stack words, byte-addressed memory, storage, returndata, and gas accounting. Exceptional halts cover invalid instructions, stack faults, invalid jumps, and out-of-gas. Legacy JUMP/JUMPI destinations must be a JUMPDEST instruction in the current code, never a byte inside PUSH immediate data. w1nt3r's evm-from-scratch supplies a test-driven opcode ladder.

proposedTopics.title: Yul syntax & the assembly block
proposedTopics.description: Yul is an intermediate language with functions, `let` variables, `if`/`switch`/`for`, literals, and dialect-provided builtins. Solidity's `assembly { ... }` uses the EVM dialect of Yul and can access selected surrounding Solidity identifiers. Inline assembly bypasses Solidity safety checks; raw arithmetic, calldata access, and memory management are the author's responsibility, though the Yul optimizer and compiler still transform and validate the language.

proposedTopics.title: Solidity memory layout & the free memory pointer
proposedTopics.description: Solidity reserves 0x00–0x3f as scratch space, stores the free-memory pointer at 0x40 (initially 0x80), and reserves 0x60–0x7f as a zero slot that must not be written. Manual allocation reads 0x40, uses an appropriately aligned region, and advances the pointer. Some compiler temporaries larger than scratch space may use memory at the free pointer without advancing it, so unallocated memory is not guaranteed to remain zero.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/FreeMem.sol write assembly that allocates one aligned word by reading and advancing the 0x40 pointer, captures that post-allocation pointer, stores a sentinel there, then performs abi.encode; test in test/phase08/FreeMem.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves the captured pointer is exactly the initial pointer plus 0x20, abi.encode does not overwrite the allocated sentinel, and the zero slot at 0x60 remains zero.

proposedTopics.title: Decoding calldata in Yul
proposedTopics.description: The EVM dialect exposes calldataload, calldatacopy, and calldatasize. For a standard external ABI function call, bytes 0–3 hold the selector and the encoded argument tuple starts at byte 4. Static values occupy 32-byte head words; a dynamic head word is an offset relative to the start of that tuple, pointing to length and data in the tail. Opcode reads beyond calldata are zero-padded, so manual decoders must enforce the ABI bounds and canonical-shape checks they rely on.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase08/CalldataYul.sol decode a (uint256,address) pair by hand with calldataload at offsets 4 and 0x24, and a dynamic bytes arg via its tuple-relative offset; test valid encoding plus truncated heads and out-of-bounds dynamic tails in test/phase08/CalldataYul.t.sol. Done when: forge test matches abi.encode on valid input, rejects each malformed low-level call, and you can explain why calldataload itself zero-pads rather than reverting.

proposedTopics.title: Reverting with data in assembly
proposedTopics.description: `revert(offset, size)` returns a memory slice as failure data, rolls back the current frame's changes, and preserves unused gas. A selector-only custom error can be left-aligned in a word and reverted over four bytes; arguments must follow standard ABI encoding. After a failed subcall, copying `returndatasize()` bytes with RETURNDATACOPY and reverting over that exact slice bubbles the failure payload.

Done when: forge test passes catching the right selector and the forwarded child reason (not an opaque revert(0,0)).

proposedTopics.title: Yul objects & the deploy/runtime split
proposedTopics.description: A Yul object contains one `code` section and zero or more named data or nested object sections. A deployable pattern uses the outer code as init code and a nested object as runtime code; the init code obtains the nested object's bytes with dataoffset/datasize, copies them with datacopy, and returns them. `solc --strict-assembly` compiles standalone Yul object notation.

proposedTopics.title: Huff macros & manual stack management
proposedTopics.description: Huff exposes EVM opcodes directly and inlines `#define macro` bodies. `takes(n)` and `returns(m)` annotate a macro's intended stack effect, while the programmer still reasons about concrete stack order and DUP/SWAP use. The current huff2 compiler adds checks for duplicate definitions, duplicate labels, and macro argument counts, but stack correctness and termination still require opcode-level review. Huff is appropriate when measured bytecode or gas constraints justify that responsibility.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What happens, to state and to gas, when a call frame runs out of gas mid-execution?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The frame halts exceptionally: its state changes are discarded, it produces no output, and its remaining gas becomes zero. Pitfall: EIP-150 caps requested CALL-family gas to all but one sixty-fourth of the gas available after call costs; a value-bearing CALL also adds a 2300-gas stipend, so forwarding is not simply `gasleft()*63/64`.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do signed and unsigned opcodes differ, and what does DIV by zero do?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Unsigned (DIV/LT/GT/MOD) treat words as 0..2²⁵⁶−1; signed (SDIV/SLT/SGT/SMOD) treat them as two's-complement. DIV/SDIV/MOD by zero return 0 — no revert at the opcode level. Pitfall: a raw uint8/address on the stack can carry dirty high bits; compare/mask before trusting it, since opcodes operate on full 256-bit words.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Give the raw opcodes that push 3 and 2 and add them.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: PUSH1 0x03 PUSH1 0x02 ADD → leaves 0x05 on the stack (ADD pops the two operands, pushes the sum).

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why can writing to a high memory offset cost far more than writing near 0x80?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The active range rounds up to 32-byte words, and expansion from a to b words costs Cmem(b)−Cmem(a), where Cmem(x)=3x+⌊x²/512⌋. Pitfall: MSTORE writes 32 bytes, so a write at offset+1 overlaps the preceding word; use MSTORE8 for one byte.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly that stores a value at 0x80 and reads it back.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { mstore(0x80, v) let x := mload(0x80) } — MSTORE writes the 32-byte word at 0x80, MLOAD reads it. Pitfall: 0x80 is the first free byte; don't write into 0x00–0x7f (scratch + free-pointer + zero-slot) without care.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do TSTORE/TLOAD differ from SSTORE/SLOAD in cost and lifetime?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: TLOAD and TSTORE each cost 100 gas, have no refund, share contract-owned state across that contract's frames, and are discarded at transaction end; TSTORE is forbidden under STATICCALL. Persistent SLOAD is 2100 cold/100 warm, while SSTORE depends on original/current/new values plus a possible cold surcharge and capped refund. Pitfall: transient writes made by a reverting frame are also reverted.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a transient-storage reentrancy guard in assembly.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { if tload(0) { revert(0,0) } tstore(0,1) } _; assembly { tstore(0,0) } — sets a transient lock, runs the body, then clears it. TLOAD/TSTORE each cost 100 gas. Transaction-end cleanup is not a substitute for clearing: a stale lock blocks later calls in the same transaction.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Contrast CALL, DELEGATECALL, and STATICCALL by storage, msg.sender, and value.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: CALL: target's own storage, msg.sender = caller, can pass value. DELEGATECALL: caller's storage, msg.sender & msg.value preserved from the outer call, no value arg. STATICCALL: like CALL but any state change (SSTORE/LOG/CREATE/value) reverts. Pitfall: a call to a codeless address returns success=true with empty returndata — EXTCODESIZE-check when you need real code; delegatecall to untrusted code hands over your storage.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Give the address formulas for CREATE and CREATE2 and the practical difference.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: CREATE: keccak256(RLP(deployer, deployer_nonce))[12:], precomputable when the nonce is known. CREATE2: keccak256(0xff ‖ deployer ‖ salt ‖ keccak256(init_code))[12:]. Pitfall: init_code includes encoded constructor arguments, so changing one changes the CREATE2 address; successful init code's returned bytes become runtime code.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the Solidity that computes a CREATE2 address for known salt and init code.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: address a = address(uint160(uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(bytes1(0xff), deployer, salt, keccak256(initCode)))))); — take the last 20 bytes of the keccak of 0xff‖deployer‖salt‖keccak256(initCode).

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do RETURN and REVERT differ, and what does EXTCODESIZE return during a constructor?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Both return a memory range, but REVERT rolls back the frame and preserves unused gas while RETURN completes normally; STOP returns empty output, and an invalid instruction is an exceptional halt that leaves the frame no gas. Pitfall: EXTCODESIZE is zero while an account's init code is running, so contract-rejection checks based on code size are bypassable from a constructor.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Building an EVM interpreter from scratch
proposedPrompts.promptText: What state does a minimal EVM interpreter track per call frame, and what must JUMP validate?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A program counter, a 1024-deep stack of 256-bit words, byte-addressed memory, gas remaining, and the last returndata — plus references to storage and world state. JUMP/JUMPI must land on a JUMPDEST (0x5b) that is a real instruction, not a byte inside PUSH data. Pitfall: failing to exclude PUSH-immediate bytes from valid jump destinations lets crafted bytecode jump into data.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Building an EVM interpreter from scratch
proposedPrompts.promptText: Pass the w1nt3r evm-from-scratch test ladder through the JUMP group.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Fork the repo, implement STOP/PUSH/arithmetic/DUP/SWAP, then JUMP/JUMPI with JUMPDEST validation; run the provided tests per opcode group.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What safety does an assembly block give up compared to Solidity?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: No overflow/underflow checks, no array bounds checks, no automatic memory management, and no type checking on values written back to Solidity variables. Pitfall: writing a value with dirty high bits into an address/bool variable from assembly can break later comparisons — mask to the type width yourself.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Solidity memory layout & the free memory pointer
proposedPrompts.promptText: What lives at 0x00–0x3f, 0x40, and 0x60 in Solidity's memory model?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: 0x00–0x3f is scratch space; 0x40 stores the free-memory pointer, initially 0x80; 0x60–0x7f is a zero slot that must not be written. Pitfall: compiler temporaries can use space at the free pointer without advancing it, so unallocated memory is not guaranteed zero and manual allocations must update 0x40.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Solidity memory layout & the free memory pointer
proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly that allocates 32 bytes using the free memory pointer.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { let p := mload(0x40) mstore(0x40, add(p, 0x20)) mstore(p, v) } — read the pointer at 0x40, bump it by the size, then use the region.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Where do a function's arguments start in calldata, and what does an out-of-range calldataload return?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Arguments start at offset 4 (after the 4-byte selector); each static arg is a 32-byte word, dynamic args store a 32-byte offset in the head with length+data in the tail. Pitfall: calldataload past calldatasize returns zero-padded bytes (not a revert), so hand-decoding short calldata can read attacker-friendly zeros as valid args — solc's ABI decoder adds the bounds checks you lose.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write Yul that loads the first uint256 argument from calldata.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: let a := calldataload(4) — the selector occupies bytes 0–3, so the first 32-byte argument word begins at offset 4 (the second is at 0x24).

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do you bubble a child call's exact revert reason back up in assembly?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: returndatacopy(0, 0, returndatasize()) then revert(0, returndatasize()) — copy the callee's returndata into memory and revert over it. Pitfall: revert(0,0) discards all error data (opaque failure); to raise your own custom error, store shl(224, selector) plus encoded args and revert over that range.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly that reverts with a 4-byte custom-error selector.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { mstore(0x00, shl(224, 0x12345678)) revert(0x00, 0x04) } — put the selector in the top 4 bytes of the word at 0x00 and revert over those 4 bytes.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How is a standalone Yul object structured, and what does its init code do?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An outer object = creation/init code with a `code{}` and a nested sub-object ("runtime") whose `code{}` is the deployed code; the init code datacopy's the runtime and RETURNs it. Pitfall: forgetting to RETURN the runtime from the constructor deploys empty code, and dataoffset("runtime") must match the sub-object's name.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What do takes/returns mean in a Huff macro, and what enforces them?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: They annotate the macro's intended number of consumed and produced stack items. You still manage actual item order and DUP/SWAP behavior against the inlined opcodes. Pitfall: treating the annotation as a substitute for tracing all control-flow paths can leave a caller with the wrong stack shape.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a Huff macro that adds one to the top stack item.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: #define macro ADD_ONE() = takes(1) returns(1) { 0x01 add } — pushes 1 and ADDs it to the existing top-of-stack value.
